macro.analysis: Capital markets remain broadly supportive of the AI sector, but that support is not indiscriminate. The AI Equity Index edged up to 33.0, positive one-year returns cover 63.2% of tracked companies and broad financial conditions remain loose. At the same time, Reuters reports that Anthropic’s IPO prospectus has intensified attention to AI valuations, while CNBC reports that higher bond yields have increased risk for debt-hungry AI companies. The aggregate backdrop remains favorable, but valuation and funding are receiving greater scrutiny at individual firms. The physical expansion is large, but the power pipeline remains a filter between proposed and operating capacity. Available records show 1,556 data-center sites in development, equal to about half the operating base. The active interconnection queue contains 2,061 GW, yet only 24.2% has reached the executed-agreement or construction stages; just 13% of the 2000–2020 queue cohort ultimately became operational. That historical rate is not a forecast for today’s projects, but it shows why queue size alone overstates deliverable capacity. S&P Global also reports that data centers are compounding transmission congestion. The economic case for this investment ultimately depends on deployment and measurable gains. Businesses reporting current AI use account for 23.8%, with 27.6% expecting to use it within six months. Nonfarm-business productivity grew 2.2% and real output grew 2.5%, but those aggregate figures do not isolate AI’s contribution. The tracked labor channels remain narrow: only one has positive employment growth, and only two have positive real-earnings growth. Adoption is meaningful, but these measures do not yet establish a broadly distributed labor-market or economic payoff from AI.
